<reason>Side B (PRO) opened with a clean three-pillar case plus durability, and its best original move — the cliff-edge family that direct certification cannot reach, plus the "squeezed tray still feeds, a cut program feeds no one" asymmetry — remained live. But Side A (CON) did more damaging comparative work at every contested node. A converted the stigma pillar into a solvable design problem (cashless lines, universal serving lines, direct certification), and B's concession that funding-side income data, file records and pull-outs survive universalism [B4.1] left B claiming only the register-level visibility that A plausibly showed is already obtainable without universalism. A dissolved the cliff-edge into a phase-out/sliding band and pointed out that every policy has a boundary; B never engaged the phase-out mechanism, merely reasserting "someone still sits one dollar past it," which is much weaker against a tapering subsidy. A's pressure question demanding B ring-fence summer feeding, breakfast and food quality extracted an honest but costly answer ("I won't pretend budgets are infinite... a matter of how a legislature prioritizes"), which A then weaponized effectively as "the objection restated as a hope." B's fair reply that CON assumes a fixed pie was asserted but never developed with any mechanism for new appropriations. On durability, B's asymmetry framing was its strongest rhetorical asset, but A blunted it twice: nobody proposed abolishing school lunch, so "zero tray" is a phantom, and universal degradation is regressive because the child with a stocked fridge absorbs none of the loss. A also landed the crisp meta-comparison — B's case rests on speculation about future legislatures, A's objection is arithmetic. B's closing largely re-ran the cliff and durability lines without answering the phase-out or the funding concession. A's Rebuttal 1 being clipped for length is a genuine execution cost, but the truncated content was recovered later.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Q2 demanding a commitment that no dollar be taken from summer feeding, breakfast, or food quality, and B's answer that budgets aren't infinite and prioritization is a legislative choice — A turned that honest concession into the debate's decisive line, showing PRO's cost defence was a hope rather than a rebuttal.</best_rebuttal>
